Two closed wooden trunks used to carry masks and costumes sit on the bare ground between the poles. To the left stands a Gujarati village schoolmaster of about forty, clean-shaven, in a plain white dhoti and a buttoned white cotton bandi jacket over a collarless shirt, his head bare; his face is an ordinary invented face shown in three-quarter view, never a portrait likeness of any real person. He stands with quiet, grave resolve, one hand reaching forward, placing a small fold of plain rupee notes into the open palm of a second man facing him. This second man is the troupe's nayak, its leader: sturdy, moustached, dressed in plain everyday travelling clothes — a coloured cotton kurta and a loosely tied waist-cloth, with no stage make-up or costume on him this morning — an ordinary invented face, listening with his head tilted slightly and his free hand resting on his hip. Behind the two men, a few tile-roofed and thatched village houses stand at a distance beyond a large neem tree, with a stretch of green tobacco field visible past them. No crowd, no children, no other figures anywhere — only the two men in a quiet, private exchange. Soft warm morning sunlight, plain rural ground, a serious and deliberate mood, neither a performance nor a celebration.
